Title: Fascial closure after open abdomen: initial indication and early revisions are decisive factors--a retrospective cohort study.

Journal/Date: International journal of surgery (London, England) (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Abdomen, Abdominal Cavity, Aged, Digestive System Surgical Procedures, Fasciotomy, Female, Humans, Intestinal Fistula


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: The surgical treatment method in which the peritoneal cavity is opened anteriorly and deliberately left open, hence often called "open abdomen" has become the standard of care in damage-control procedures as well as in the management of intra-abdominal hypertension and in severe intra-abdominal sepsis. Whereas open abdomen has been closed in two stages traditionally, a modern trend is to close the fascial layers within the initial hospitalization to avoid complications like enterocutaneous fistula and hernia formation. The aim of this study was to determine crucial factors influencing the possibility of fascial closure after open abdomen.
[METHODS]: Between 2003 and 2013, 355 adult patients were treated with open abdomen in our institution. Their data were collected and retrospectively analyzed. They were divided into two groups depending on fascial closure or not (fascial closure, n = 137 (39%) vs. non-fascial closure, n = 218 (61%)).
[RESULTS]: The patients who reached fascial closure had a significantly higher rate of initially performed open abdomen (97 patients (71%) vs. 118 (54%), p = 0.002) and the periods of time until a second and a third look operation were significantly shorter (2.7 ± 2.5 vs. 4.2 ± 6.6 days, p = 0.021 and 5.6 ± 3.7 vs. 8.5 ± 8.6 days, p = 0.006). Furthermore, the presence of peritonitis (64 patients (47%) vs. 83 patients (38%), p = 0.023) and large bowel resection (74 patients (54%) vs. 90 patients (41%), p = 0.022) were significantly higher in this group. Rates of in-hospital mortality (97 patients (44%) vs. 38 patients (28%), p = 0.002) and the presence of pancreatitis (19 patients (9%) vs. 3 patients (2%), p = 0.013) were significantly higher in the non-fascial closure group.
[CONCLUSIONS]: The probability to reach fascial closure after open abdomen seems to increase when open abdomen is performed initially and when early second and third look operations are performed. The presence of pancreatitis seems to be the only negative prognostic marker concerning fascial closure.

PMID 25447607; DOI 10.1016/j.ijsu.2014.11.025. It was published electronically 25 Nov 2014 and in the January 2015 issue.
This was a single-institution retrospective cohort of 355 adults treated with open abdomen from 2003–2013, comparing fascial closure (137/355, 39%) with non-closure (218/355, 61%).

The paper frames initial open abdomen use around damage-control procedures, intra-abdominal hypertension, and severe intra-abdominal sepsis. The abstract does not provide a complete categorized table of all initial indications; it reports that an initially performed open abdomen was more common among patients who ultimately achieved fascial closure (97 [71%] vs 118 [54%], p=0.002).

Early revision timing was strongly associated with closure: time to second-look operation was 2.7±2.5 versus 4.2±6.6 days (p=0.021), and time to third-look operation was 5.6±3.7 versus 8.5±8.6 days (p=0.006), closure versus non-closure respectively. Other between-group findings included more peritonitis (47% vs 38%, p=0.023) and large-bowel resection (54% vs 41%, p=0.022) in the closure group, while pancreatitis (9% vs 2%, p=0.013) and in-hospital mortality (44% vs 28%, p=0.002) were higher in the non-closure group.

The authors concluded that fascial closure probability appears to increase when open abdomen is performed initially and second- and third-look operations are conducted early; pancreatitis appeared to be the only negative prognostic marker for closure. Thus, within this retrospective dataset, initial indication/strategy and early revision timing were considered decisive or important factors, but the evidence is observational and the abstract provides no adjusted multivariable effect estimates.
